idiom_name: structuredClone/spread copy published with one property or store assignment
implementation_notes: JavaScript values are references and = binds names, so the pattern survives as its ordering: build the complete next value (structuredClone for a deep copy, spread plus slice/concat for a shallow update with structural sharing) and publish it with a single assignment -- a property write, a Map.set, or the store's own setState. Nothing observable changes until that one publish, so a throw while building (a DataCloneError, a validation error in a factory) leaves the current value untouched, and the previous graph stays valid for readers that already hold it until the collector reclaims it. Where an in-place commit is genuinely required, Object.assign(target, built) or a collection's replace-style API installs a fully built value into the existing identity, which is the closest thing to the swap half; there is no copy constructor to hook, and class instances need a hand-written clone/with method.
pitfalls: Spread and Object.assign are shallow: nested objects stay shared, so writing through the 'copy' changes the original and breaks reference-equality change detection in frameworks such as React.

structuredClone deep-copies but discards the prototype chain (a class instance comes back as a plain object), does not preserve property descriptors, getters or private class elements, and throws DataCloneError on functions and DOM nodes.
Object.freeze is shallow and only prevents replacing properties: array elements, Map/Set contents and nested objects remain mutable, so freezing alone does not make a published snapshot safe.

The publish looks atomic in a single-threaded runtime, but async code interleaves between build and assignment: for a read-modify-write, re-read inside the store's updater (setState(prev => ...)) instead of closing over a stale snapshot.
